We often fit surrogate models so that we can use them in optimization problems. We want the conditions that
maximize a predicted yield, the design that minimizes a predicted cost, or the next
experiment to run. With a black-box model that usually means a local optimizer and
some restarts, and at the end you have an answer with no way to know whether a better
one exists somewhere you did not look. This is a well-known weak point of
surrogate-based optimization [@bhosekar2018surrogate; @cozad2014alamo].

There is a class of models where you can do much better. Some surrogates are
*piecewise linear* once they are trained: networks built from affine maps and ReLUs,
Kolmogorov-Arnold networks with linear splines, regression trees with linear leaves,
and sparse regressions on hinge functions. A piecewise-linear function can be written
*exactly* as a set of mixed-integer linear constraints. The trained model then becomes
part of a mixed-integer linear program (MILP), and a MILP solver returns the **global**
optimum of the model together with a proof that nothing better exists inside the input
box. Better still, the surrogate is now just one block in an optimization model, so you
can add your own constraints, integer decisions and other models around it.

Over the past few months we have added this capability to four of our packages:
[pycse](https://github.com/jkitchin/pycse) (most of the `pycse.sklearn` models),
[jax-ldt](https://github.com/jkitchin/jax-ldt) (linear and hyperplane decision trees),
[jax-difftree](https://github.com/jkitchin/jax-difftree) (differentiable soft trees),
and [jaxsr](https://github.com/jkitchin/jaxsr) (symbolic regression). This post
explains why you would want it, how the models get into a solver, and what each package
offers, including the limitations.

The figure below shows the problem and the solution on a small example. The surrogate
is a ReLU network with one input and 17 hidden units, so it is piecewise linear with one
kink per unit, and it has four valleys. The deepest one is narrow. Press *5 random
starts* to run local search (here, exact steepest descent along the curve): each start
slides into the nearest valley and stops, and with these starts none of them finds the
deepest one. Nothing in the result tells you that a better answer exists. Then *Step*
through branch and bound. In the MILP, each ReLU has a binary variable, and in one
dimension deciding a binary is the same as deciding which side of that unit's kink $x$
lies on, so each branch splits the interval at a kink. On each piece, the units whose
kink is outside the piece are fixed and the rest are relaxed, which gives a lower bound
(the green segments). Any piece whose bound is above the best point found so far
cannot contain the minimum, so it is discarded. When no pieces are left, the best
point is proved to be the global minimum. Real MILP solvers bound with LP relaxations,
which are tighter than the interval bounds used here, but the logic is the same.

## Why global optimization of the surrogate matters

The usual way to optimize a neural network or a smooth tree is gradient-based:
start somewhere, follow the gradient, restart a few times. That works when the
surrogate is nearly convex. When the surrogate has several basins, which is
common for exactly the response surfaces we care about (selectivity versus
temperature and pressure, cost versus a handful of design variables) you have
little control over which one you find. The jax-difftree docs say it plainly:
inverse design over a soft tree is local, and multistart is the practical
fallback.

A MIP solver works differently. It bounds the objective over regions of the input
space and discards regions that cannot contain the optimum. When it finishes, the
optimality gap is zero (or a tolerance you chose), and that is a statement about the
whole box, not about the neighborhood of a starting point. For smooth networks you can
get the same guarantee from deterministic global MINLP solvers
[@schweidtmann2019global], but for piecewise-linear models the problem is a MILP, and
MILP solvers are fast, mature and free (HiGHS [@huangfu2018highs] solves every MILP in
this post).

There is a second reason that matters just as much in practice. A surrogate embedded
as constraints composes with everything else. You can put two unit-operation
surrogates in one flowsheet, add a budget constraint, choose between discrete
equipment options, and still get a global optimum of the combined problem. A
`predict` function cannot do that.

## What "MIP-representable" means

The building block is the ReLU, $y = \max(0, a)$. If you know bounds
$L \le a \le U$ with $L < 0 < U$, one binary variable $d$ encodes it exactly:

$$
y \ge 0, \qquad y \ge a, \qquad y \le a - L(1 - d), \qquad y \le U d.
$$

When $d = 1$ the constraints force $y = a$, and when $d = 0$ they force $y = 0$. This
is the big-M formulation, and it has been used for trained ReLU networks for some time
[@fischetti2018deep; @tjeng2019evaluating; @grimstad2019relu]. Stronger formulations
exist [@anderson2020strong], and @vielma2015mixed is a good general reference. The
same idea covers hinge terms $\max(0, x - k)$, absolute values, linear splines (with
SOS2 or segment binaries), and tree routing (one binary per leaf).

Two consequences follow from that formulation and show up in every section below.
First, **the bounds $L$ and $U$ come from bounds on the inputs**, propagated through the
model. Every input must have finite bounds, and tight bounds give small big-M
constants, which gives fast solves. Loose bounds are the most common cause of a slow
MILP. Second, the formulation is exact only for piecewise-linear pieces. A SiLU, tanh
or softplus activation, a cubic spline, or a polynomial term is not piecewise linear,
and you either retrain with a piecewise-linear choice or move to a nonlinear solver.

It helps to name the levels of representability, since not every model lands in the
same place.

| Level            | What it means                                                    | Examples                                                                |
|------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Exact LP         | No binaries needed                                               | Linear models; input-convex networks when the output is minimized       |
| Exact MILP       | Reproduces the model to solver precision                         | ReLU networks, linear-spline KANs, linear-leaf trees, hinge regressions |
| Approximate MILP | Some 1D nonlinearity interpolated on a grid, with an error bound | pycse's periodic network (sin/cos features)                             |
| Exact MINLP      | The model is written as its own nonlinear equation               | SISSO equations, jaxsr models with `allow_nonlinear=True`               |

Uncertainty adds one more ingredient. For several pycse models the predicted standard
deviation is a second-order cone in the network's internal variables, so robust
objectives like $\mu + 2\sigma$ become mixed-integer second-order cone programs. We come
back to this in the pycse section.

## Getting a surrogate into a solver

There are three routes from a trained model to an optimization problem, and our
packages use all of them.

**Direct Pyomo embedding.** The model writes its own variables and constraints into a
[Pyomo](https://www.pyomo.org/) `Block` [@bynum2021pyomo]. You pass in your own Pyomo
variables as inputs, and the block links them to the surrogate. This is the most
flexible route and the one every package here supports (`to_pyomo` in pycse, jaxsr and
jax-difftree, `embed_in_pyomo_model` in jax-ldt). Any Pyomo MILP solver works: HiGHS,
Gurobi, CPLEX, SCIP.

**OMLT.** [OMLT](https://github.com/cog-imperial/OMLT) [@ceccon2022omlt] reads a neural
network (usually from ONNX) and builds a Pyomo block with a choice of formulations, such
as `ReluBigMFormulation`. OMLT also has tree formulations, including linear model
decision trees [@ammari2023linear]. In our packages, pycse's `LLPRRegressor` exports to
ONNX and directly to an OMLT `NetworkDefinition` (`to_onnx()`, `to_omlt()`). One
caveat: jax-ldt also writes ONNX, but OMLT cannot read it. OMLT's ONNX reader
understands neural-network layers (Gemm, MatMul, ReLU), and the tree-routing operations
(Gather, LessOrEqual) are rejected. That is why the tree packages ship their own
adapters.

**discopt.** [discopt](https://github.com/jkitchin/discopt) is our hybrid MINLP solver
with a JAX backend. jax-ldt (`embed_in_discopt_model`) and jaxsr (`to_discopt`) write
directly into a `discopt.Model`, and jax-difftree reaches discopt through the jax-ldt
spec (more on that below). The advantage of discopt is that the same model can hold
MILP surrogate blocks and nonlinear constraints, which is where jaxsr's
`allow_nonlinear=True` and pycse's SISSO export are headed. pycse itself writes
Pyomo, but the ONNX file from `LLPRRegressor.to_onnx()` can also be read by
`discopt.ml.load_onnx`.

Whatever the route, the pattern is the same: declare bounded input variables, embed the
surrogate, add your constraints, set an objective on the surrogate output, solve, and
then check the answer against the model's own `predict`.

## pycse.sklearn models

pycse has the broadest coverage. A new module in pycse 2.13.0, `pycse.sklearn.mip`,
holds the
formulation machinery once, and each estimator only describes its trained weights. A
model implements `mip_network()`, which returns its weights as plain numpy layer specs
(`Affine`, `ReLU`, `PiecewiseLinear`), a `TreeModel` of leaf boxes, or a symbolic
expression. A single function, `add_to_pyomo`, turns any of these into constraints, so
the bound propagation, the big-M formulation and the tests are shared across models.
For the user it is one call:

```python
import pyomo.environ as pyo
from pycse.sklearn import DPOSE

model = DPOSE(layers=(2, 32, 16)).fit(X, y)       # ReLU by default

m = pyo.ConcreteModel()
m.T = pyo.Var(bounds=(300, 500))
m.P = pyo.Var(bounds=(1, 10))
m.budget = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.T / 100 + m.P <= 12)   # your own constraints
m.nn = pyo.Block()
model.to_pyomo(block=m.nn, inputs=[m.T, m.P])        # input bounds come from your vars
m.obj = pyo.Objective(expr=m.nn.y[0], sense=pyo.maximize)
pyo.SolverFactory("highs").solve(m)
```

Internal input and output scaling is folded into the exported weights, so `m.T`, `m.P`
and `m.nn.y` are in your units.

### Which models, and what they need

| Model | Requirement | Level | Binaries | Std exported |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `DPOSE` [@kellner2024dpose] | `activation=nn.relu` (default) | MILP | ≤ 1 per ReLU unit | yes (ensemble) |
| `LLPRRegressor` [@bigi2024llpr] | `activation="relu"` | MILP | ≤ 1 per ReLU unit | yes (LLPR) |
| `NNBR` | `MLPRegressor(activation="relu")` | MILP | ≤ 1 per ReLU unit | yes (Bayesian ridge) |
| `KfoldNN` | `activation="relu"` (default is swish) | MILP | ≤ 1 per ReLU unit | yes (ensemble) |
| `JAXICNNRegressor` [@amos2017icnn] | `activation="relu"`, `strong_convexity_mu=0` | MILP, or LP | 0 with `formulation="convex"` | no |
| `JAXMonotonicRegressor` | `activation="relu"` | MILP; LP if `convexity="convex"` | ≤ 1 per ReLU unit | yes (LLPR) |
| `KAN` [@liu2024kan] | `spline_order=1`, `base_activation="linear"` | MILP | ~`grid_size` per layer input | with `n_ensemble > 1` |
| `KANLLPR` | `spline_order=1`, `base_activation="linear"` | MILP | ~`grid_size` per layer input | yes (LLPR) |
| `LeafModelRegressor` | a linear `leaf_model` | MILP | 1 per leaf in the box | no |
| `LinearRegressionUQ` | none | LP | 0 | yes |
| `JAXPeriodicRegressor` | `activation="relu"` | approximate MILP | grid segments + ReLUs | yes |
| `SISSO` [@ouyang2018sisso] | none (TorchSisso to fit) | MINLP | 0, nonlinear | yes |

"One binary per ReLU unit" is an upper bound. Units that are always on or always off
over the input box need no binary, and interval bound propagation finds them. A DPOSE
network with 32 hidden units needed 30 binaries in the docs notebook.

A few of the formulations are worth a sentence each. KAN layers apply a 1D spline to
every edge, but all the edges leaving one input share its breakpoints, so the MIP uses
one SOS2 set per *input* rather than per edge. Trees use one binary to pick a leaf, and
leaves that lie outside the input bounds are dropped before the MIP is built. Leaf
models are recovered by probing `predict` and then checked at random points, so any
linear scikit-learn pipeline works and a nonlinear one raises an error.

Input-convex networks get special treatment. In an input-convex ReLU network every
hidden unit reaches the output through nonnegative weights, so when the output is
*minimized*, the two lower inequalities $y \ge 0, y \ge a$ are enough: the solver pushes
each unit down to $\max(0, a)$ on its own. `formulation="convex"` drops all the
binaries and the problem becomes an LP. pycse checks the weights first and refuses
networks that are not convex.

### How it performed

To test the exports we fitted six models to the same 400 noisy samples of
$f(x) = \tfrac14\lVert x\rVert^2 + \sin 3x_1 + \cos 2x_2 + 0.15x_2$ on the square
$[-2, 2]^2$, then minimized each model with HiGHS. The function has one global minimum,
$f^* = -1.599$ at $(-0.50, -1.43)$, and several local ones. The deepest of these is a
mirror-image well at $(-0.50, 1.36)$ with $f = -1.181$, the obvious place for a model to
go wrong. The results answer three questions. (They come from one run. Different
training runs shift the numbers a little, but not the conclusions.)

**Is the MIP exact?** Yes. For every model, the MIP minimum was equal to or slightly
below the minimum of a 301×301 grid search on the same model, which is what a true
global minimum must do. Evaluating the model with its own `predict` at the MIP's
answer reproduced the MIP objective to $10^{-11}$ or better.

**Is the answer right?** Yes, when the model is good. These fits have test RMSE between
0.07 and 0.11, and every one of their MIP optima landed in the global well, within 0.14
of $f^*$ when judged by the true function. None of them fell into the second well. The
figure below shows where each one landed. A model has to be good enough for this. With
300 training epochs `LLPRRegressor` underfit (RMSE 0.24), and its optimum missed $f^*$
by 0.5, so we trained it for 1000. All six models predict a minimum slightly *deeper*
than the true one (between $-1.69$ and $-1.83$). That is expected: a global optimizer seeks out the
places where the model's error happens to be most negative, so the predicted value at
the optimum is biased low. Check the optimum against the real function before you
trust the number.

**What does it cost?** The number of binaries grows with the size of the network, and
the solve time grows faster than that:

| Model | Binaries | Solve (s) |
|---|---|---|
| KfoldNN (32, 16) | 29 | 0.06 |
| DPOSE (32 hidden units) | 29 | 0.10 |
| KAN (2, 4, 1), grid 10 | 68 | 0.29 |
| KANLLPR (2, 4, 1), grid 10 | 66 | 0.55 |
| LLPRRegressor (32, 32) | 63 | 8.1 |
| NNBR (32, 32) | 59 | 9.3 |

The two networks with two hidden layers of 32 units are the slow ones. KANs have about
as many binaries but solve much faster, because their binaries come from splines on the
inputs rather than from stacked ReLU layers. The convex formulation is cheaper still: on
a convex test function, `JAXICNNRegressor` (64, 64) took 0.47 s with 122 binaries as a
MILP and 0.06 s with no binaries as an LP, and both found the same minimum.

We left the tree (`LeafModelRegressor`) out of this comparison. On a smooth function
like this one, 400 points are not enough for a tree to fit well (test RMSE 0.29 or
more), and its optimum missed $f^*$ by 0.9 to 2.7 depending on the settings. The MIP
still finds the tree's minimum exactly; the tree is just a poor model of $f$ here.

to show that model's surface.

### Optimizing with uncertainty

For every pycse model with a standard deviation, the std has the form
$\sigma(x) = \sqrt{\lVert A z(x) + c \rVert^2 + d}$, where $z$ is one layer of the
network (the ensemble members for DPOSE and KfoldNN, the last-layer features for the
LLPR models). That is a second-order cone. `to_pyomo(include_std=True)` adds a
variable with $s \ge \sigma(x)$, which is convex and exact whenever the objective
*penalizes* the std, as in robust design ($\min\ \mu + 2\sigma$).
`include_std="exact"` enforces $s^2 = \sigma(x)^2$ instead. It is nonconvex, and it is
needed when the objective *rewards* the std, as in exploration for active learning
($\min\ \mu - 2\sigma$), because with the cone alone that problem is unbounded.

| Objective | Mean at x* | Std at x* | MIP objective | Grid | Solve |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| mean | -1.7826 | 0.1024 | -1.7826 | -1.7800 | 0.36 s |
| robust: mean + 2 std | -1.7693 | 0.0932 | -1.5830 | -1.5792 | 0.21 s |
| explore: mean - 2 std | -1.7769 | 0.1076 | -1.9923 | -1.9900 | 4.2 s |

Penalizing the std trades a little mean for less uncertainty, and rewarding it does the
opposite. Both std options need a solver with quadratic constraints (Gurobi, CPLEX,
SCIP). These numbers are a separate DPOSE fit from the docs notebook, solved with Gurobi; `pip install gurobipy` includes a
size-limited license that covers small examples like this.

### Caveats

You have to choose piecewise-linear options at training time. Several pycse defaults
are smooth (LLPR, ICNN, monotonic, periodic and KfoldNN, plus KAN's cubic splines), and
`to_pyomo()` raises a `ValueError` naming the setting to change. The accuracy cost of
ReLU or linear splines is usually small, but it is a retraining step.

MIP size grows with the network. Two hidden layers of 32 units solved in 7 to 15 s
here, and much larger networks may not solve in reasonable time. KANs (binaries per
input, not per unit) and the convex LP scale better.

The convex LP is one-sided: it is exact only when the output is minimized or bounded
above. To maximize an ICNN, use the MILP.

Periodic models are approximate. The sin/cos features are interpolated on a grid, with
a per-feature error of at most $(2\pi/n)^2/8$ for $n$ points per period (4.8e-3 at the
default of 32). The MIP finds the global optimum of the *interpolated* model, which in
the notebook landed 2.4e-3 above the grid-search minimum of the un-interpolated model at 8 to 32
points. At 64 points it beat the grid search, at the cost of 288 binaries instead of
160.

Trees have a boundary problem. A tree sends $x \le t$ left, and a MIP cannot express the
strict inequality on the other side, so a point exactly on a split can take either
leaf's value. `split_gap=1e-4` excludes a thin slab above each split. The gap has to be
well above the solver tolerances; at 1e-6 HiGHS still picked the wrong leaf.

SISSO exports exactly, but the equation is nonlinear (division, exp, log), so it needs a
global MINLP solver such as BARON, SCIP or Gurobi's nonlinear mode. Ipopt will only find
a local optimum.

`ZENNRegressor` and `ZENNClassifier` are not representable (their output is a
log-sum-exp over sub-networks). `NNGMM`'s mean network could be exported but is not
wired up yet, and `JAXICNNRegressor` with `strong_convexity_mu > 0` would be a MIQP but
is not exported.

The walkthrough is the pycse docs page
[Optimizing over machine-learned models with MIP](https://kitchingroup.cheme.cmu.edu/pycse/docs/mip.html).
The code is in [`mip.py`](https://github.com/jkitchin/pycse/blob/master/src/pycse/sklearn/mip.py)
(its module docstring has a worked example), with tests in
[`test_sklearn_mip.py`](https://github.com/jkitchin/pycse/blob/master/src/pycse/tests/test_sklearn_mip.py),
and a KAN versus ReLU size comparison in
[`KAN_Demo.ipynb`](https://github.com/jkitchin/pycse/blob/master/src/pycse/examples/KAN_Demo.ipynb).

## jax-ldt: linear and hyperplane decision trees

[jax-ldt](https://github.com/jkitchin/jax-ldt) fits linear-model decision trees, where
every leaf holds a linear regression instead of a constant, and hyperplane trees, where
the splits are oblique hyperplanes chosen from sparse combinations of the inputs. Both
are piecewise linear by construction, so they were designed from the start to be
embedded. The package was motivated by our work with the Laird group on hyperplane trees
as surrogates for chemical process design [@sunshine2025hyperplane], which builds on
linear model decision trees in OMLT [@ammari2023linear]. Optimization over tree models
more generally goes back to @misic2020optimization and ENTMOOT
[@thebelt2021entmoot].

The MILP formulation lifts the features into the transformed (hyperplane) space, uses
one binary per leaf, writes the routing as big-M constraints, and linearizes the leaf
outputs with big-M as well. The result is an exact MILP. The same formulation is
available in Pyomo and in discopt:

```python
import discopt
from jax_ldt import HyperplaneTreeRegressor
from jax_ldt.export import embed_in_discopt_model

model = HyperplaneTreeRegressor(max_depth=4, max_bins=6, min_samples_leaf=15)
model.fit(X, y)

m = discopt.Model("min-y")
x = m.continuous("x", shape=(2,), lb=-2, ub=2)
y_expr = embed_in_discopt_model(model, m, x)
m.minimize(y_expr[0])
result = m.solve()
```

For Pyomo, `embed_in_pyomo_model(model, m, m.x)` builds the same formulation on a
sub-block, so several trees can share one model. For axis-aligned trees with constant
leaves there is also a lighter adapter, `to_discopt_decision_tree`, which uses discopt's
built-in tree formulation.

The canonical export is a JSON spec (`to_json` / `from_json`), and every other format is
regenerated from it. That turns out to be useful beyond jax-ldt, because jax-difftree
writes the same spec.

**Caveats.** Big-M constants are derived per node and per leaf from the input bounds,
so bounds are required. You can override them with `big_m=`, and they are validated
when the inputs are bounded. The ONNX export is for inference with onnxruntime, not for
OMLT, as noted above. The tree's uncertainty estimates are stored in the spec but are
not part of the MILP.

Docs: [MIP export](https://github.com/jkitchin/jax-ldt/blob/main/docs/mip_export.md),
[discopt integration](https://github.com/jkitchin/jax-ldt/blob/main/docs/discopt_integration.md).
Examples: [`04_mip_optimization.ipynb`](https://github.com/jkitchin/jax-ldt/blob/main/examples/04_mip_optimization.ipynb),
[`07_pyomo_embedding.ipynb`](https://github.com/jkitchin/jax-ldt/blob/main/examples/07_pyomo_embedding.ipynb).

## jax-difftree: differentiable soft trees

[jax-difftree](https://github.com/jkitchin/jax-difftree) takes a different route to a
tree. Instead of growing it greedily, it fits a fixed-depth *soft* tree end to end with
gradients [@hehn2020end], with oblique splits and sigmoid routing. Soft trees are smooth
and train well, and they can match derivative data (Jacobians from a simulator) as well
as values. They are not piecewise linear, though, so getting a MILP takes one extra step.

The workflow is to train with affine leaves, harden the tree so that each point routes
to exactly one leaf, and then export the crisp piecewise-affine model:

```python
from difftree import DifferentiableTreeRegressor, export
import pyomo.environ as pyo

model = DifferentiableTreeRegressor(
    depth=3, leaf_type="affine", jacobian_weight=1.0, hardening=True
)
model.fit(X_tr, Y_tr, dydx=J_tr)
print(model.hardening_report_)            # soft vs hard error, before and after

m = pyo.ConcreteModel()
m.x = pyo.Var(range(2))
m.y = pyo.Var(range(2))
tree = export.to_pyomo(model, m, x=m.x, y=m.y, bounds=(lo, hi), method="bigm")
m.obj = pyo.Objective(expr=m.y[0])
pyo.SolverFactory("appsi_highs").solve(m)
```

The Pyomo export is written as a generalized disjunctive program: each leaf is a
`Disjunct` holding its polytope and its affine model, and a `Disjunction` makes exactly
one leaf active, which Pyomo then transforms (here with big-M). For discopt,
`export.to_json` writes the jax-ldt v1 spec, so jax-ldt's `from_json` and
`embed_in_discopt_model` consume a difftree model unchanged. All outputs share one
partition, which means a multi-output tree for a unit operation needs only one set of
binaries.

**Caveats.** The *soft/hard gap* is the main one. The MILP optimizes the hardened tree,
not the soft one you trained, so check `soft_hard_gap` (and train with `hardening=True`) before
trusting the optimum. The leaf polytopes are closed, as usual in big-M formulations, so
an optimum can sit on a split boundary using either neighbor's model;
`export.repair_solution` moves such a point into the chosen leaf. Continuity across
oblique splits needs `tied_splits=True`, which gives up flexibility (a depth-$D$ tree
then has $D$ hyperplanes instead of $2^D - 1$). The fixed full-binary structure caps
practical depth at around 10 to 12. A pruned export matches `predict(hard=True)` only
inside the export box.

Docs: [surrogates for MILP](https://github.com/jkitchin/jax-difftree/blob/main/docs/surrogates.md),
[limitations](https://github.com/jkitchin/jax-difftree/blob/main/docs/limitations.md).
Notebooks: [`piecewise_linear_milp`](https://github.com/jkitchin/jax-difftree/blob/main/notebooks/piecewise_linear_milp.ipynb),
[`pyomo_embedding`](https://github.com/jkitchin/jax-difftree/blob/main/notebooks/pyomo_embedding.ipynb),
[`multivariate_inverse_design`](https://github.com/jkitchin/jax-difftree/blob/main/notebooks/multivariate_inverse_design.ipynb).

## jaxsr: symbolic regression with hinge functions

[jaxsr](https://github.com/jkitchin/jaxsr) fits sparse symbolic models, a weighted sum
of terms chosen from a basis library by an information criterion, in the spirit of ALAMO
[@cozad2014alamo]. The new capability is a family of piecewise-linear basis terms,
most usefully hinges $\max(0, x - k)$ and $\max(0, k - x)$, which give MARS-style fits
[@friedman1991mars; @breiman1993hinging]. If every selected term is piecewise linear,
the fitted model is an exact MILP, and unlike the other models in this post it is also a
short, readable equation.

```python
from jaxsr import BasisLibrary, SymbolicRegressor, milp_incompatible_terms

library = (
    BasisLibrary(n_features=2, feature_names=["T", "P"], feature_bounds=[(0, 4), (0, 4)])
    .add_constant()
    .add_linear()
    .add_hinges(X=X, n_knots=7)
    .add_transcendental(["abs"])
)
model = SymbolicRegressor(basis_library=library, max_terms=6, information_criterion="bic")
model.fit(X, cost)
print(model.expression_)
print(milp_incompatible_terms(model))   # [] means a pure MILP
```

The MILP-representable terms are constants and linear terms (written directly), hinges
and `abs` (one binary each, big-M), categorical indicators (one-hot binaries), and
categorical-continuous interactions (an exact McCormick product). The model then goes
to either backend with one call, linked to your own variables:

```python
model.to_pyomo(m.sr, inputs={"T": m.T, "P": m.P}, output=m.cost)   # Pyomo block

emb = model.to_discopt(dm_model)                                    # discopt
dm_model.subject_to(emb.inputs["T"] + emb.inputs["P"] >= 5)
dm_model.minimize(emb.output)
```

Polynomials, interactions, `log`, `exp` and the rest are not piecewise linear. You can
still embed them with `allow_nonlinear=True`, which gives an MIQCP or MINLP for discopt,
BARON, SCIP or Gurobi.

**Caveats.** Bounds are required and are *enforced* on the embedded inputs, on purpose:
outside the training range the model is extrapolating, and the right fix is more data,
not wider bounds. Knot placement matters more than knot count, since the fit can only
bend where a knot exists, so pass known breakpoints (a phase boundary, a saturation
point) explicitly with `knots=`. Parametric and custom basis functions, rational forms
and SISSO-style features cannot be embedded. `MultiOutputSymbolicRegressor` is not
supported directly, but each `estimators_[i]` can be embedded separately. The embedding
is built from the fitted coefficients, so rebuild it after a refit.

Guide: [Embedding models in MILPs](https://github.com/jkitchin/jaxsr/blob/main/docs/guides/mip-embedding.md).
Example: [`mip_surrogate_optimization.ipynb`](https://github.com/jkitchin/jaxsr/blob/main/docs/examples/mip_surrogate_optimization.ipynb),
which includes a refine-and-resolve loop and a design problem solved in both backends.

## Choosing a model

<!-- TODO: optionally run one shared benchmark through all four packages for a fair
comparison of fit error, MILP size and solve time. -->

The packages overlap, but they are good at different things. If you want an
interpretable equation, or you know where the response bends, jaxsr's hinge models are
the natural choice, and they stay small. If you want a flexible fit with uncertainty and
the option of a robust or exploratory objective, the pycse ReLU networks are the most
complete, and the input-convex networks are the cheapest to optimize when convexity is
physically justified. Trees are attractive when the response has genuinely different
regimes: jax-ldt grows them greedily and exports directly, while jax-difftree trains
them end to end, can use derivative data, and needs the hardening step before export.

| | pycse ReLU nets | pycse KAN | jax-ldt | jax-difftree | jaxsr hinges |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Binaries scale with | hidden units | grid × inputs | leaves | leaves ($2^D$) | hinge/abs terms |
| Interpretable | no | partly | partly | partly | yes |
| Std in the MIP | yes (SOCP) | with LLPR/ensemble | no | no | no |
| Pyomo | yes | yes | yes | yes (GDP) | yes |
| discopt | LLPR via ONNX | no | yes | via jax-ldt spec | yes |
| OMLT | LLPR via ONNX | no | no | no | no |

## The caveat that applies to all of them

A global optimizer finds your model's mistakes. Our first run of the pycse benchmark
used 150 samples and shorter training. Two of the models came out poorly fitted, and
their global optima sat on the edge of the box, where there was little data and the
models were extrapolating: one predicted $-1.58$ at a point where the true $f$ is
$+1.07$. A local optimizer started in the middle might
never go there, and the MIP always will. The global optimum of the *surrogate* is only
as good as the surrogate is in that region. So validate the optimum against the true
model, and then either add data there and refit (jaxsr's notebook has a refine-and-resolve
loop, and our earlier [active-learning post](../surrogate-active-learning/) covers the
data side), penalize the std, or tighten the bounds to the region you trust.

## Installing

The MIP export is in pycse 2.13.0 and later. Pyomo and HiGHS come with the `mip` extra;
the ONNX and OMLT exports of `LLPRRegressor` also need `onnx` and `omlt`.

```bash
pip install "pycse[mip]"
```

jaxsr 0.3.0 is on PyPI, but the hinge terms and MILP embedding are newer than that
release, so install from GitHub for now. jax-ldt and jax-difftree are not on PyPI. (The
`difftree` package on PyPI is an unrelated project, so install jax-difftree from GitHub
as shown.)

```bash
pip install "jaxsr[mip] @ git+https://github.com/jkitchin/jaxsr.git"
pip install "jax-ldt[pyomo] @ git+https://github.com/jkitchin/jax-ldt.git"
pip install "difftree[pyomo] @ git+https://github.com/jkitchin/jax-difftree.git"
pip install discopt omlt onnx
```
